strengths: The presentation is quite clear, and the design of TAMU is simple and easy to understand.
While there are few works focused on efficient unimodal deployment, this appears to be the first adaptation in audio-visual speech tasks. The motivation is therefore innovative.

A novel approach to utilize information from two or more modalities at model training time to improve run-time performance when only a single or a subset of modalities are present. Proposed approach relies on estimating, in a time aligned manner, modality features that are not present at run-time.
Proposed model is parameter and compute efficient
Results in a significant accuracy gains without adding too many parameters over the baseline unimodal model.

The authors present a potential method to guide the projection from audio to visual representation when visual input is absent. However, the experiments are insufficient and lack persuasiveness. The writing is clear and well-structured.
The paper presents a useful approach to multimodal-to-unimodal distillation through its use of codebooks for modality alignment.
The technical work includes benchmarking across different datasets and tasks, with testing under various noise conditions and SNR levels.
The authors provide ablation studies on codebook sizes and architectural choices, and show how their method works with different baseline architectures.
The experimental results are well-documented, and the paper's structure makes it easy to follow their methodology and findings.
From a practical standpoint, the work offers a solution for running multimodal systems with single modality inputs during deployment.
Their implementation reduces model size by 80% and requires less computation compared to full multimodal systems.

The authors' method for aligning audio and visual dimensions works effectively, and they demonstrate good performance across benchmarks while keeping the model compact in terms of parameters and MACs.
The results suggest their approach could be useful for applications where resource efficiency matters.
weaknesses: The paper needs to provide a more detailed analysis of the trade-offs between performance gains and the practical costs of deploying audio-visual systems, including industry statistics and concrete scenarios where added visual complexity is justified.

The paper does not discuss the potential impact of temporal misalignment between audio and video streams on the performance of the TAME module; it is unclear how the model handles situations where audio and visual cues are not perfectly synchronized, which is common in real-world scenarios.

It is uncertain how general TAME is; the paper should explore the adaptability of TAME to different visual modalities such as lip movements or facial expressions, and provide a more comprehensive analysis of its limitations and potential for generalization across different types of visual data.

The claim that "visual modality is the most widely used in these speech tasks" needs empirical evidence, as text appears to be more prevalent; the paper should provide supporting data for this assertion.

The paper should acknowledge that multimodal input can sometimes be detrimental, especially when the modalities are not perfectly aligned or when one modality is noisy or unreliable, and discuss this critical issue in the challenges of multimodal learning.

The related work section should consider "ReVISE: Self-Supervised Speech Resynthesis with Visual Input for Universal and Generalized Speech Enhancement," indicating the literature review needs to be more comprehensive.

Missing baselines: Using multiple modalities at training time only to improve performance under a single or a subset of modalities has been studied before (e.g., [1]). References & comparison with those methods needs to be carried out to fully assess the merits of the proposed model.

Only the case of audio-visual ASR / Speech enhancement / Active speaker selection is studied, providing a limited bi-modal view of general multimodal tasks; a more general multi-modal setting would make this work much more attractive.

The author conducted experiments solely on the audio-visual dataset, comparing the performance of the multi-modal, audio-only, and MUTUD frameworks, but no independent validation and comparison with other models were carried out on out-of-domain audio-only datasets, making it difficult to assess generalizability.

Lack of novelty: similar methods have already been explored, such as "Multi-modality Associative Bridging through Memory: Speech Sound Recollected from Face Video," which predicts audio features from visual features; the paper does not sufficiently highlight the unique aspects of the proposed TAME module compared to existing methods.

The performance gain is quite limited compared to the audio-only model; the marginal improvements raise questions about the added complexity of the proposed method and the need for a more thorough analysis of the trade-offs between performance gains and computational overhead.

The experimental evaluation lacks a comprehensive comparison with state-of-the-art models across the three tasks considered (AV speech enhancement, AV active speaker detection, and AV speech recognition), making it difficult to gauge the relative performance of the proposed method.

The evaluation of the TAME module is limited to relatively older backbone models; it is unclear how TAME would perform when integrated with more recent and advanced backbone architectures, limiting its applicability and potential impact.

A main motivation of this paper (motivation 2) is rather weak; a video camera available in even the cheapest smartphone is not "complex sensory devices working together seamlessly", and other modalities like text are not explored.

It is unclear how MUTUD could generalise to other settings; the paper focuses on audio-visual training with only audio during inference and does not consider the reverse scenario (only video at inference time).

The methods section is extremely short, and the majority of the work in this section is not the authors’ own; the codebooks definition lacks contribution and citation, and the loss functions are uncited, making the overall technique a direct application of others' work rather than a significant contribution.
Experiments compare to only two methods (one adapted audio method from 2019 and one adapted audio-visual method from 2023); this limited baseline comparison is insufficient to meet ICLR requirements.

There is no empirical justification as to why estimating visual features from audio features is better than simply using only the audio features; the codebook methodology should be used in multiple settings to support this claim.
The paper should compare to a list of contemporary methods (at least 6: 3 audio-only and 3 audio-visual); current comparisons are insufficient.
The number of parameters and MACs have very little influence on inference speed, yet the paper lacks inference time metrics despite the narrative focusing on efficiency.
The paper does not break down how the parameters and MACs are allocated across components (e.g., audio codebook, video codebook, training size, evaluation size).
The tables are not well labelled; it is often unclear what the evaluation task is for each table and on which dataset, requiring digging through paragraphs of experimental detail.
